design_detail: Field study that the authors call a cohort study with a between-groups design (JAMA Psychiatry 2020), Colorado, registered as an observational study (NCT03522103). Adults who already used cannabis flower or concentrates regularly were measured before and after using a legal-market product that they bought themselves: within each form (flower or concentrate), the labelled THC strength was assigned by random-number table (flower 16% or 24%; concentrate 70% or 90%), but the form itself was each person’s own choice. After a baseline visit and 5 days of using the product, a mobile laboratory came to the participant’s home; blood, self-rated intoxication and mood, cognitive tests and balance were measured before use, about 13 minutes after use and 1 hour after use, with the person using the product in the way they preferred in between. No placebo or no-use session, and nobody who does not use cannabis.
can_establish: What was measured in 121 regular consumers before and after they used a legal-market product at home: blood THC and its active metabolite 11-OH-THC were higher in the concentrate group than the flower group at every time point; self-rated intoxication and most cognitive tests did not differ by form or by labelled strength within form at the authors’ threshold (P < .01); delayed verbal recall and eyes-closed balance were worse after use in both groups, with balance back to its pre-use level by 1 hour. It gives measured blood levels after naturalistic use of products as sold, which controlled studies with lower-strength study cannabis do not.
cannot_establish: Whether concentrates cause more or less impairment than flower: people chose their own form, the two groups differed at baseline in how often they used concentrates, how long they had used cannabis regularly and in baseline THC metabolite, there was no placebo or no-use session so practice and the passage of time cannot be separated from the drug, and each person chose how much to use. Effects in people who use cannabis less often or are new to it (inclusion required use at least four times in the past month and earlier use of the strongest product without a bad reaction), long-term effects (follow-up was 1 hour), driving or other real-world performance, dependence, mental health, or any effect on the lungs or other organs. Why self-rated intoxication matched despite different blood levels is not shown: tolerance, receptor saturation and individual differences are the authors’ suggestions, untested. Strength was the labelled THC percentage; other cannabinoids and contaminants are not reported.

sample.recruitment: Social media postings and mailed flyers advertising to people who use flower or concentrates (Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph). Participants were paid $50 for the baseline visit and $100 for the mobile-laboratory visit; no funds were provided for buying cannabis, so each person paid for their own study product. Self-selected volunteers.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: age 21 to 70; cannabis at least 4 times in the past month; earlier use, at least once by self-report, of the strongest product that could be assigned (24% THC flower or 90% THC concentrate) with no adverse reaction; no other non-prescription drug in the past 60 days (urine screen); no daily tobacco; alcohol no more than twice a week and no more than 3 drinks an occasion; not pregnant or trying to become pregnant; not treated for a psychotic or bipolar disorder (Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph). Twelve of the 133 people assessed were removed afterwards because blood THC after use was below 0.02 µg/mL (study mean 0.24, SD 0.35), taken to mean they had not used the product at home and returned at once as instructed (Results › Descriptive Information): 9 of 64 flower (14%) and 3 of 69 concentrate (4%) participants (editors’ arithmetic).
sample.demographics: Analysed: flower group 55, mean age 28.8 (SD 8.1), 42% women; concentrate group 66 (65 with baseline data), mean age 28.3 (SD 10.4), 48% women (Table 1). White 78% and 79%; bachelor’s degree or higher 64% and 45%; prescribed psychiatric medication 4% and 12%. Baseline cannabis use, flower vs concentrate group: days of concentrate use in the past 30 days 3.5 vs 16.5; days of flower use 20.6 vs 15.4; age at start of regular use 20.0 vs 17.7 years; cannabis use disorder symptoms 2.96 vs 3.09; baseline plasma THC 0.004 vs 0.009 µg/mL and THC-COOH 0.044 vs 0.087 µg/mL. Alcohol use 7.4 vs 9.0 days and tobacco use 0.5 vs 1.8 days in the past 30.
sample.attrition: 133 assessed, 12 excluded after the visit because of low post-use blood THC (9%), 121 analysed; the Abstract says these 121 complied with instructions and had complete data across the primary outcomes. One concentrate participant had no baseline demographic data (Table 1 footnote); 30-day use history was missing for some flower participants (41 of 55 present, Table 1 footnote).
sample.selection_effects: Strong. Volunteers who already used cannabis regularly, had used the strongest product before without a bad reaction and agreed to be tested at home; people who were new to cannabis or used it rarely, had had an adverse reaction to a high-strength product, used tobacco daily or other drugs, or were treated for psychosis or bipolar disorder were excluded, so the findings cannot be carried over to them or to people who do not use cannabis. Excluding people because their blood THC after use was very low removes the low end of one of the outcomes themselves, and removed more of the flower group (14%) than the concentrate group (4%). Products came from one dispensary that set aside allotments for the study.

exposure.measurement: Form and labelled THC strength (flower 16% or 24%, concentrate 70% or 90%) as tested by an ISO 17025-accredited laboratory and labelled as Colorado requires; purchase verified by receipt; product weighed before and after use at the session; mode of use recorded (concentrate group: glass rig or tube 92%, hash pen 8%; flower group: pipe 51%, bong 31%, vaporizer 11%, joint 7%). Plasma THC and 11-OH-THC by liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry (Methods › Primary Measures › Blood Cannabinoids).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: A single ad libitum session at home, after 5 days of free use of the study product, with the route chosen by the participant. Product used at the session, mean (SD): flower 0.22 g (0.18), concentrate 0.11 g (0.14) (Table 1); by labelled strength: flower 24% 0.24 g, 16% 0.19 g; concentrate 90% 0.10 g, 70% 0.13 g, reported as not significantly different within form. Mean time away from the mobile laboratory 13.3 minutes (SD 7, range 3 to 47). Other cannabinoids (for example CBD) and contaminants not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Limited by selection: no other non-prescription drug in the past 60 days (urine screen), no daily tobacco, light alcohol use, breath alcohol tested before the session. Tobacco and alcohol use in the past 30 days were low in both groups (tobacco 0.5 vs 1.8 days, alcohol 7.4 vs 9.0 days). Tobacco mixed into joints is not recorded (4 of 55 flower participants used joints).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Asked not to use cannabis on the day of the visit before the first (pre-use) measurement; median pre-use blood THC was 0.003 µg/mL (range 0 to 0.05) (Figure 1 legend).

comparison.controls: No placebo and no no-use session (the authors say placebo products do not exist on the legal market) and no group of people who do not use cannabis. Three comparisons: before against after use within each person; flower group against concentrate group (self-selected, not randomised); higher against lower labelled strength within each form (random assignment).
comparison.matching: None between forms. Each model included the baseline value of the outcome as a covariate; removing it did not change the pattern. Random assignment to strength within form gave groups that did not differ except in race among the concentrate groups (P < .01) (Table 1 footnote).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tolerance and length of regular use differ between the form groups and are only partly captured (concentrate use on about 16 of the past 30 days against about 3, regular use started about two years earlier, baseline THC-COOH about twice as high). The authors name interactions that were not tested or accounted for: strength and cannabinoid ratio, mode of use, expectancies and smoking technique (Limitations).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Light alcohol and no other drug use by selection; groups similar on alcohol and tobacco days (Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: Plasma THC and 11-OH-THC; Addiction Research Center Inventory marijuana scale (12 items); a 3-item intoxication scale (mentally stoned, physically stoned, feeling high); Profile of Mood States vigor and tension subscales; 30-minute delayed verbal recall (International Shopping List Task); NIH Toolbox inhibitory control (flanker), working memory and episodic memory (picture); quiet-standing balance on a smart device with eyes open, eyes closed, and eyes closed with head tilted back (Methods › Primary Measures). Details are in eMethods (Supplement 2, not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Intoxication scale Cronbach alpha 0.69. The marijuana effects scale correlated 0.42 with the intoxication scale and 0.46 with tension (Results › Subjective Drug Effects). Validity of the smart-device balance measure is not described in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Change from before use to about 13 minutes after use (short-term) and 1 hour after use, tested with linear and quadratic time terms in repeated-measures analysis of variance, with form and form-by-time interactions; strength within form tested in the supplement. Impairment is inferred from change in the same person, with no placebo comparison.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: A fixed, stricter threshold of P < .01 set in advance for the number of outcomes (Methods › Statistical Analysis). Thirteen outcomes, each with five tests in Table 2 (linear time, quadratic time, form, form by linear, form by quadratic), is about 65 tests, plus the strength tests in the supplement; a fixed threshold, not a formal correction (a Bonferroni threshold for 13 outcomes would be about .004). Several results fall between .01 and .05 (verbal recall form by quadratic P = .02; eyes-open balance P = .05).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Participants were not masked to product strength (federal rules restricted masking, Limitations), and the self-rated outcomes depend on what people expect.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (SE) before, about 13 minutes after, and 1 hour after use (Table 2). Blood THC µg/mL: flower 0.004, 0.14, 0.02; concentrate 0.01, 0.32, 0.03; form effect F(1,228) = 11.00, P < .01; form by quadratic F = 15.07, P < .001. 11-OH-THC µg/mL: flower 0.001, 0.005, 0.004; concentrate 0.004, 0.011, 0.008; form effect F = 46.82, P < .001. Intoxication scale: flower 0.08, 2.40, 1.93; concentrate 0.14, 2.35, 1.63; form effect F(1,230) = 2.57, P = .11. ARCI marijuana scale: form effect F = 1.84, P = .18. Tension and vigor lower in the concentrate group (P < .01, P < .001). Delayed verbal recall errors: flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33; linear change F(1,203) = 32.31, P < .001; form effect P = .65; form by quadratic P = .02. Eyes-closed sway: flower 0.63, 0.73, 0.63; concentrate 0.64, 0.69, 0.64; quadratic time F(1,203) = 18.88, P < .001; form effect P = .85. Inhibitory control higher in the flower group at every time (P < .001); inhibitory control and working memory scores rose over the session (linear P < .001), which the authors suggest may reflect practice; episodic memory no effect. Eyes-open balance quadratic P = .05; eyes-closed head-back no change. Strength within form: no effects in the main text (eResults and eTables, Supplement 2, not read). No confidence intervals or standardized effect sizes.
analysis.covariates: Baseline value of each outcome in every model. Race compared across groups but not entered in any model. No adjustment for the baseline differences between the flower and concentrate groups in recent concentrate use, years of regular use or THC metabolite.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Registered as an observational study at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03522103; the protocol is Supplement 1 (PDF, not opened) and the registry record was not opened, so whether outcomes, threshold and comparisons match the registered plan was not checked. The paper says a second primary outcome of the larger study, change in inflammation markers, will be reported elsewhere (Methods › Primary Measures › Blood Cannabinoids).
analysis.selective_reporting: All 13 outcomes appear in Table 2 with all five effects each, including null results and results against the hypothesis (for example higher tension and vigor in the flower group). Strength results are only in the supplement. The exclusion of 12 people was decided from the blood result. Not in the main text: confidence intervals, effect sizes, individual-level data.
analysis.power: No power calculation in the main text (protocol and supplement not read). With 55 and 66 people overall and about 26 to 33 per strength group, absence of a significant difference is weak evidence of no difference, and the paper gives no interval showing how large a difference the data rule out.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 121 adults who already used cannabis at least four times a month, blood THC measured about 13 minutes after self-administered use was higher in the concentrate group than in the flower group (mean 0.32 against 0.14 µg/mL), and 11-OH-THC was higher at every time point. Self-rated intoxication, the marijuana effects scale and most cognitive tests did not differ by form, and nothing differed by labelled strength within form at P < .01. Delayed verbal recall and eyes-closed balance worsened after use in both groups; balance had returned to its pre-use level by 1 hour. Tension and vigor were lower in the concentrate group at every time point, and inhibitory control scores were higher in the flower group at every time, including before use. The concentrate group had used concentrates on far more days, started regular use about two years earlier and had about twice the baseline THC metabolite. There was no placebo, so changes after use cannot be separated from repeating the tests; follow-up was 1 hour.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract says short-term use of concentrates was associated with higher THC exposure and that verbal memory and postural stability were associated with THC across forms and strengths, which the data support. The Conclusions add that THC exposure was much higher in the concentrate group, prompting concern about long-term clinical and neurobehavioral implications, and the Key Points describe concentrates as associated with potentially greater risk; neither long-term outcomes nor clinical outcomes were measured. The Discussion reads the lack of a blood-level difference by strength within each form as suggesting self-titration (an inference from non-significant differences in groups of 26 to 33), offers tolerance, receptor saturation and individual differences as untested explanations for equal intoxication at different blood levels, and proposes that balance impairment could mark recent use. The authors state the main limits: no random assignment to form, no placebo, limited control of dosing and masking.

timeline.event: Same group: survey of people who use concentrates on the legal market, with strength and health-related outcomes (Bidwell et al., Addictive Behaviors Reports; cited as reference 6, not read).
This study: naturalistic use of legal-market flower and concentrates, measured in a mobile laboratory; the authors present it as the first of its kind (Discussion, 1st paragraph).
Systematic review of cannabis potency and mental ill health and addiction (Petrilli et al.); not yet readable for this library; will be added.
Scoping review and evidence map of high-concentration cannabis products in this batch (Bero et al.); it maps what has been studied and does not appraise the studies.

replication.where_it_stands: One study from one research group in one state; no second measurement of blood THC and impairment after naturalistic use of concentrates and flower was read for this batch. Controlled studies of smoked and vaporized flower under set dosing (Spindle 2018, this batch) measure a different question in people who rarely use cannabis.

funding.funder: US National Institutes of Health (grant DA039707 to Hutchison) and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (grant 96947 to Bidwell). The funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation or the decision to submit (author-information panel, funding and role of the funder).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Bidwell reports grants from NIH/NIDA and from the State of Colorado (CDPHE); Ellingson reports NIH funding; Klawitter reports CDPHE and NIH; Sempio reports CDPHE and NIH; Bryan reports NIH and the State of Colorado; no other disclosures. No cannabis-industry funding or ties are declared. Participants bought their products from one local dispensary, which set aside allotments for the study; no payment from the dispensary is declared.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Colorado Boulder (Psychology and Neuroscience; Institute for Cognitive Science), University of Colorado Aurora (Psychiatry; Anesthesiology) and Colorado State University; blood assays at the iC42 laboratory, Anschutz Medical Campus. Several authors also wrote the 2018 survey of concentrate use that the paper cites. The Colorado grant comes from the same state health department that funded Monte 2019 (this batch). Recorded as a reason to read closely, not to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study that follows people over time or assigns the form: for example the same people using flower and concentrate on different days, with measured product content beyond THC percentage, a placebo or no-use session to separate practice from drug effects, people with different amounts of experience including those new to cannabis, and longer follow-up of driving-relevant performance, dependence and mental-health outcomes over months to years.

domains.note: Form was chosen by participants. The concentrate group used concentrates on about 16 of the past 30 days against about 3, started regular use about two years earlier and had about twice the baseline THC-COOH, so tolerance and history differ; these are not adjusted for beyond the baseline value of each outcome. Random assignment to strength protects only the within-form comparison.

Product, labelled strength (laboratory tested), weighed amount and mode of use are recorded, which is better than most field studies; but the amount is each person’s choice, labelled THC is not measured content, other cannabinoids and contaminants are not reported, and 12 of 133 people were removed because blood THC was too low to show they had used the product as instructed.

Self-selected volunteers who already used cannabis regularly and had used the strongest product before without a bad reaction; excluding 12 people by their post-use blood THC, one of the outcomes, removed more of the flower group (9 of 64) than the concentrate group (3 of 69); no one new to cannabis or using it rarely.
Measurements followed a fixed sequence; nothing after use is described that would change outcomes differently by group.

Complete data on the primary outcomes was a condition of analysis (121 of 133); 30-day use history is missing for some flower participants and one concentrate participant lacks baseline demographics; handling of other missing values is not described.

Blood cannabinoids are measured by validated chromatography with mass spectrometry. Intoxication and mood are self-rated by people who knew their product’s strength and the study’s hypothesis (modest scale reliability, alpha 0.69). Tests were repeated three times within about an hour with no placebo or practice-control session, so practice effects cannot be separated from drug effects (the authors raise this for two tasks). Validity of the smart-device balance measure is described only in the supplement.

Registered as an observational study with the protocol in Supplement 1 (not compared here); a fixed P < .01 threshold across 13 outcomes; results between .01 and .05 are described in words as trends or marginal, and not consistently across text and legends; strength results sit in the supplement and a second primary outcome is to be reported elsewhere.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is applied to a cohort-style field study. Confounding and selection are judged high because the central comparison (flower against concentrate) is between self-selected groups that differ in prior use and probably tolerance, there is no placebo or no-use session, and 12 people were removed using the blood result; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. Against that: laboratory-tested products, weighed use, blood cannabinoids at three time points, a registered design, a deliberately strict significance threshold, and null results shown in full. It can be cited for measured blood THC after naturalistic use of legal-market flower and concentrates in regular consumers, and for the absence of detectable differences in self-rated intoxication and short-term tests at one hour; it cannot be cited for long-term outcomes, for people who use cannabis less often, or for a causal comparison of the forms.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7287943 (author manuscript; Key Points, abstract, Methods, Results, Tables 1 and 2, Discussion, Limitations, Conclusions, reference list and the author-information panel read as text; Figures 1 to 3 are images, their legends were read and their values not extracted; Supplement 1 (protocol) and Supplement 2 (eMethods, eResults, eTables, eFigures) are PDFs and were not opened)

key_findings.finding: 133 people were enrolled and assessed (64 flower, 69 concentrate); 12 were removed because blood THC after use was below 0.02 µg/mL (study mean 0.24), leaving 121 (55 flower, 66 concentrate); mean age 28.8 and 28.3 years; 42% and 48% women.
key_findings.locator: Results › Descriptive Information, paragraph; Abstract; Table 1
key_findings.note: The Abstract gives 25 women (46%) and 30 women (45%); Table 1 gives 23 (42%) and 31 (48%).

key_findings.finding: Within each form, participants were randomly assigned a labelled strength (flower 16% or 24% THC; concentrate 70% or 90% THC), bought it at one dispensary, used it freely for 5 days, then used it in their preferred way at home during a mobile-laboratory visit; measures were taken before use, about 13 minutes after use (mean 13.3, range 3 to 47) and 1 hour after use.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Experimental Appointment, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mean blood THC after use was 0.32 µg/mL in the concentrate group and 0.14 µg/mL in the flower group; 11-OH-THC reached 0.011 and 0.005 µg/mL; both were higher in the concentrate group at every time point, including before use, and THC had fallen to 0.03 and 0.02 µg/mL by 1 hour. No difference by labelled strength within form.
key_findings.note: The Abstract and Results label 0.43 and 0.16 as standard errors; the Discussion gives them as standard deviations.

key_findings.finding: Self-rated intoxication rose to similar levels in both groups (short-term mean 2.40 flower, 2.35 concentrate; form effect P = .11); so did the marijuana effects scale (P = .18). Tension and vigor were lower in the concentrate group at every time point (P < .01 and P < .001). No associations with labelled strength.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Delayed verbal recall errors rose after use in both groups (linear effect P < .001; flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33 before, short-term and 1 hour after); form effect P = .65, form by quadratic time P = .02 (above the .01 threshold). Inhibitory control (flanker) was higher in the flower group at every time point (P < .001); inhibitory control and working memory scores rose over the session, which the authors suggest may reflect practice.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurobehavioral Performance › Cognition, paragraph; Table 2; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Eyes-closed sway increased after use and returned to its pre-use level by 1 hour in both groups (quadratic P < .001; form effect P = .85); eyes-open balance showed a trend (P = .05); the eyes-closed head-back condition did not change. The authors describe about 11% more sway and compare it with the effect of moderate alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurobehavioral Performance › Balance, paragraph; Table 2; Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: At baseline the concentrate group reported concentrate use on 16.5 of the past 30 days against 3.5, started regular use at 17.7 against 20.0 years, and had baseline THC-COOH 0.087 against 0.044 µg/mL; the amount used at the session was 0.11 g against 0.22 g; the concentrate group used a glass rig or tube (92%) or hash pen (8%); the flower group used a pipe (51%), bong (31%), vaporizer (11%) or joint (7%).

The authors give three possible explanations for similar intoxication despite higher blood THC (greater tolerance in the concentrate group; receptor saturation; individual differences in metabolism or sensitivity) and say future research must test them; they read the lack of a blood-level difference by strength within each form as suggesting self-titration.

Stated limits: no random assignment to form (ethical reasons), so pre-existing group differences may partly account for the findings; no placebo control (none on the legal market); federal rules restricted control of dosing and masking to strength; interactions of strength, cannabinoid ratio, mode of use, expectancies and technique were not tested.

Conclusions: delayed recall and balance impairment were associated with short-term use even in regular consumers; the concentrate group showed similar or lower subjective intoxication and short-term impairment than the flower group; THC exposure was much higher in the concentrate group, prompting concern about long-term clinical and neurobehavioral implications.
key_findings.note: Long-term and clinical outcomes were not measured.

reporting_issues.issue: Mean blood THC after use is printed as 0.32 (SE 0.43) and 0.14 (SE 0.16) µg/mL in the Abstract and Results; the Discussion gives the same numbers as standard deviations, and the standard errors in Table 2 are 0.02 to 0.03.
reporting_issues.consequence: 0.43 and 0.16 are standard deviations, not standard errors; the means are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The numbers of women differ between the Abstract (25 of 55 flower, 46%; 30 of 66 concentrate, 45%) and Table 1 and the Results text (23, 42%; 31 of 65, 48%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 1 reports 65 concentrate participants because one had no baseline demographics.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 rows for cannabis use disorder symptoms, AUDIT, Beck Depression and Beck Anxiety totals are headed No. (%) but hold means and SDs, and the superscript letters in the table do not match the footnote list (for example the row for days of flower use carries a letter whose footnote concerns psychiatric medication).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which between-form baseline differences were tested, and at what level, cannot be read from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The intoxication scale is described with items scored 1 to 5 and 1 to 10 in the Methods, while the Figure 2 legend gives all scales a range of 0 to 4 and Table 2 means run from 0.08 to 2.40.
reporting_issues.consequence: The units of the intoxication scale cannot be checked; group comparisons are not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: Results between .01 and .05 are described inconsistently. The Figure 3 legend says a marginal effect suggested more impairment of delayed recall in the flower group (form by quadratic P = .02), while the Abstract says differing outcomes by product type were not observed (in the context of the memory and balance results) and Table 2 shows more errors in the concentrate group at 1 hour (2.33 against 1.88). Eyes-open balance (P = .05) is called a trend.
reporting_issues.consequence: Near-threshold results should be treated as unresolved; the pre-set threshold was P < .01.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract percentages for the analysed groups (41.4% flower, 49.6% concentrate) are shares of all 133 people assessed; within each form, 86% of the flower group and 96% of the concentrate group were analysed.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader could take 41.4% and 49.6% as compliance rates; exclusions fell mostly on the flower group.
